lines.text: But dearest—Did you not understand that I understood?
lines.note: Elizabeth opens by showing she has already understood his hidden meaning.

lines.text: Every day shows me more to love in you, dearest, and I open my arms as wide as I can ...
lines.note: Robert's early declaration that every day reveals more in her to love.

lines.text: How I wish for two hearts to love you with, and two lives to give to you, and two souls to bear the weight worthily of all you have given to me.
lines.note: Elizabeth wishes for two hearts and two lives to give him.

lines.text: I am your very own, dearest dearest, with you or away from you.
lines.note: Robert reassures her that he is entirely hers whether together or apart.

lines.text: I have lost my poor Flush—lost him!
lines.note: The sudden loss of Flush becomes one of their shared ordeals.

lines.text: It seems to me that you and I are at one upon the whole question,—only that I am your Flush, and he is mine.
lines.note: Elizabeth compares herself to Flush to explain why she cannot be left to the banditti.

lines.text: What a glorious dream; through nearly two years—without a single interval of blankness,—much less, bitter waking!
lines.note: Robert recalls their glorious dream of nearly two years without blankness.

lines.text: I look back, and in every one point, every word and gesture, every letter, every silence—you have been entirely perfect to me—I would not change one word, one look.
lines.note: Robert says he would not change one word or look from their past.

lines.text: I did hate so, to have to take off the ring!
lines.note: Elizabeth hates having to take off the wedding ring after the secret marriage.

lines.text: You take my words from me—I ‘exult’ in the irrevocability of this precious bestowal of yourself on me—come what will my life has borne flower and fruit—it is a glorious, successful, felicitous life, I thank God and you.
lines.note: Robert exults in the irrevocable bestowal of herself on him.

lines.text: I can bring you no flowers but I pluck this bud and send it with all affectionate devotion.
lines.note: Robert sends a bud with all affectionate devotion.

lines.text: Your letters to me I take with me, let the ‘ounces’ cry out aloud, ever so.
lines.note: Elizabeth insists on taking his letters with her despite the luggage ounces.

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Elizabeth asks if this is her last letter before they leave together.

lines.text: I begin to think that none are so bold as the timid, when they are fairly roused.
lines.note: Elizabeth's final reflection on Wilson's courage recalls her earlier fear of Wilson's timidity.
